title: Why did Yugoslavia fall apart?
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Six republics, a revered marshal, then ten years of war and a tribunal to judge the crimes. How did a country our parents knew vanish from the map?
author: ivana-toskovic

hero.hook: A country our parents grew up with, gone from the map in a decade.

blocks.text: On **1 December 1918**, just after World War I, a new state appeared in the Balkans: the [[Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes]]. It took the name Yugoslavia in **1929**. At first, the union was a survival strategy: together, these small nations carried more weight against their neighbors, Italy and Austria.

From the start, the marriage was described as forced but necessary. Serbs, Croats and Slovenes spoke almost the same language. Their religions and temperaments, however, were deeply different, and those differences soon came to the surface. Seventy years later, the country broke apart in a series of wars. How did it come to that?

sections.title: Tito, the glue of a fragile federation

blocks.text: In the Balkans, the cult of the strong leader is an old tradition. As communism rose, [[Josip Broz Tito]] came to embody it. He ruled the federation with a firm hand while staying on good terms with the Western powers and the communist world alike. Under his authority, Yugoslavia thrived.

blocks.caption: Tito (right) and his wife Jovanka Broz visiting Goričane mansion, in Slovenia, in 1967.

blocks.text: Beneath the surface, old grudges remained. Serbia had seen the union as a way to enlarge its territory, and the other nations resented its authoritarian ways. Croatia, marked by the influence of Nazi Germany, and Slovenia did not want to pay for the poorer part of the country. In **1974**, a new constitution began to weaken the federal government.

Tito died in **1980**. Nobody replaced him. When communism collapsed across Europe, nothing held the federation together anymore. In **1991**, Croatia and Slovenia declared their independence. Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in turn in **1992**.

sections.title: Economic crisis and the rise of nationalism

blocks.text: The breakup took shape in an exhausted economy: mass unemployment, runaway inflation. In that climate, politicians understood that a nationalist message paid better than defending a united Yugoslavia. In Serbia, [[Slobodan Milosevic]] gained influence by stirring up Serbian national feeling. In Croatia, Franjo Tudjman did the same on the Croatian side.

blocks.caption: A 50 billion dinar banknote, bearing the portrait of Miloš Obrenović, issued in 1993 amid hyperinflation.

blocks.text: Tensions turned into open war: every nation of the former federation ended up fighting the others, weapons in hand. The fighting killed many civilians and drove entire populations onto the roads. Faced with forced migration on this scale, the international community could no longer look away.

sections.title: Srebrenica, Storm and the Hague tribunal

blocks.text: In **1995**, the war reached its climax. In Bosnia, Serbian generals led the [[Srebrenica massacre]]: Bosnian civilians were killed en masse. A month later, the Croatian army launched [[Operation Storm]], a military offensive aimed this time at Serbian civilians. Other war crimes and massive human rights abuses struck the whole region.

blocks.caption: The white headstones of the Potočari memorial, near Srebrenica.

blocks.text: To judge these crimes, the UN Security Council created, through Resolution **827**, the [[International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia]], based in The Hague. It recognized only one genocide, Srebrenica. Yet Carl Bildt, the European Union's special envoy, described Operation Storm as one of the most efficient acts of [[ethnic cleansing]] in history. For many, these tragedies proved that the Yugoslav union had never been anything but a forced construction.

sections.title: Thirty years on: Europe or Russia

blocks.text: Some of the former republics have turned West. Slovenia and Croatia are now members of NATO and the European Union. Montenegro, whose independence from Serbia was approved by a vote in **2006**, is expected to join them soon.

Serbia, for its part, is the official successor of Yugoslavia. It remains outside the European Union and close to Russia. NATO membership seems out of the question: in **1999**, the alliance bombed Belgrade, its capital, and the memory is still raw. Depending on who is in power, coexistence between neighbors goes through calmer or rougher periods.

"Yugo-nostalgia" is a widespread feeling among older generations and in the Balkan diaspora. Many lived the best years of their lives in the federation: they traveled the world, the economy was stable, and they sincerely believed in the union of peoples and in multiculturalism.

Younger generations, meanwhile, are trying to move past the debate over war crimes. Their horizon is European integration, with the Balkans seen as a full part of the continent. Thirty years on, the question remains open: Europe or Russia?

blocks.text: A survival union born in 1918, held together by Tito and then eaten away by economic crisis and nationalism, Yugoslavia broke apart in ten years of wars whose traces the Balkans still carry.
